summary: For ages 5–7: a coast is where land meets the ocean, and coasts can be sandy, rocky, or muddy — each a different habitat with different plants and animals. This is a naming and habitat-matching topic: define 'coast' as the land–sea boundary, recognise the three shore types by what they are made of, and match a typical plant and animal to each (seaweed with crab/limpet/anemone on rock; marram grass on the dunes behind the beach with sanderling/razor shell/cockle on sand; saltmarsh plants such as samphire with curlew/lugworm on mud). These are typical examples, not strict rules: some animals, such as crabs, lugworms and wading birds, can live on more than one kind of shore. Keep it observational and photographic; tides and erosion mechanisms are saved for older learners. The core insight is that one coastline can hold three very different neighbourhoods, and each plant or animal lives where it can meet its needs.
misconceptions: 'A beach is always sandy' — not knowing rocky and muddy shores are also coasts.
'The coast is just where you swim' — missing that the coast is the meeting line of land and sea, including cliffs and mudflats.
'The same animals live on every shore' — not connecting a shore's material to which animals suit it.
Confusing coast with the open ocean, or with a river bank/lake edge.
Thinking muddy shores are 'dirty/empty' when mudflats are rich in worms and feeding birds.

activities.title: Pan the changing coastline and reveal who lives there
steps: Look at a continuous coast picture that changes along its length — golden sand, then tumbled rock, then glistening mud.
Point to the line where land meets the sea and say 'this is the coast'.
Name each stretch as sandy, rocky, or muddy by looking at what the ground is made of (not just its colour).
Tap or lift a flap on each shore to hear what makes it special: rock has cracks and water-filled pools to shelter in; sand can be burrowed into; mud is soft and full of hidden food.

Find the hidden residents: a crab wedged in a rock crevice next to seaweed, a razor shell buried in sand below the dune grass, a long-beaked bird probing the mud beside saltmarsh plants, and say each plant's or animal's name with one fact.
Say out loud why that animal is in that spot — 'the crab hides in the rock', 'the bird digs in the soft mud for worms'.
activities.insight: A coast is the line where land meets the ocean, the SAME coast can be sandy, rocky, or muddy, and each animal lives where that shore lets it hide, burrow, or feed.

activities.title: Sort the animals onto the right shore
steps: Look at three shore trays labelled sandy, rocky, and muddy.

Place (drag or physically move picture cards of) a crab, limpet, sanderling, razor shell, curlew (a long-beaked wading bird), and lugworm onto the shore where each is most often found. Some, like crabs and lugworms, can live on more than one kind of shore.
Before placing each one, say why: 'The crab goes on the rocks because it can hide', 'the curlew goes on the mud because it can probe for worms'.
Check each placement against a short 'why it fits' explanation.
activities.insight: Different shore materials suit different animals; matching an animal to a shore means thinking about what the animal needs (a place to hide, soft ground to dig, food to find).

activities.title: Say what a coast really is
steps: Answer in your own words: 'What is a coast?' — aiming for 'where land meets the ocean', not 'a sandy beach'.
Name at least two kinds of coast (sandy, rocky, muddy).
Name one animal you would expect at each kind of coast you named.
Decide whether a rocky cliff with waves at its base is a coast, and explain why.
Trace the edge where land meets the sea on a map all the way round and say whether the whole line is coast, even the parts with no people.
activities.insight: A coast is defined by the land–sea boundary (including cliffs and mudflats), not by sand or by being a holiday spot, and its type shapes which animals live there.

activities.title: Tell the ranger about your beach day
steps: Talk with a 'beach ranger' (an adult, puppet, or role-play voice) about what you have found or might find at the beach.
Describe something you saw and say which shore it came from — sand, rock, or mud.
Answer the ranger's follow-ups: 'What was the ground like there?' and 'What animal did you see, and why was it there?'
activities.insight: New coast vocabulary connects to the learner's own remembered experiences, and even a familiar beach trip can be sorted into shore types with their typical life.

checkQuestion: A child says: 'A coast is always a sandy beach — that's what a coast IS.' Is that right? Tell me what a coast really is, and whether every coast looks the same.
checkAnswer: It's not quite right — a coast is anywhere the LAND MEETS the ocean, not only a sandy beach. Coasts come in different kinds: sandy, rocky, or muddy. Each kind has different plants and animals — for example crabs and limpets on a rocky coast, or wading birds probing a muddy shore.
